column1: When can you overtake on the left?
column2: When the driver ahead has moved right and signalled right, when you have signalled left, or in slow-moving traffic where the left lane is moving faster.

column1: What is meant by a solid white line in the centre of the road?
column2: Keep left and do not cross the line except for access or in an emergency.

column1: What does a broken yellow line mean?
column2: It marks a hard shoulder, normally for pedestrians and cyclists; you may pull in briefly to let faster traffic pass if it is safe.

column1: What do double broken white lines along the centre of the road mean?
column2: They warn that continuous white lines are ahead; do not cross unless it is safe.

column1: At a stop sign that has no white line, where should you stop?
column2: At the stop sign.

column1: Where there is a continuous and a broken white line along the centre of the road, which one do you obey?
column2: The line nearest to you.

column1: Who has priority at a roundabout?
column2: Traffic already on the roundabout.

column1: When driving, when should you dip your headlights?
column2: When meeting traffic, following closely behind another vehicle, on continuously lit roads, and in poor visibility such as fog, snow, dusk, or dawn.

column1: What should you do if you are dazzled by another vehicle's headlights?
column2: Slow down and stop if necessary; watch for pedestrians and cyclists; look towards the left verge if the dazzle is from oncoming traffic.

column1: What restrictions are there in relation to the use of the horn?
column2: Do not use it in a built-up area between 11:30 pm and 7:00 am unless there is a traffic emergency.

column1: Within what distance from the kerb should you park?
column2: Within 45 cm.

column1: Where should you not overtake?
column2: Near bends, hill crests, hump-back bridges, continuous white lines, entrances, taxi ranks, or where the road is narrow or visibility is poor.

column1: What is the sequence of traffic lights?
column2: Green, Amber, Red, Red+Amber, Green.

column1: What does a clearway mean?
column2: No parking during the stated times and no stopping unless you are held up in traffic.

column1: What rules apply to a box junction?
column2: Do not enter unless you can clear it without stopping; the main exception is turning right while waiting for a safe gap without blocking traffic with priority.

column1: What is the difference between a pelican crossing and a zebra crossing?
column2: A pelican crossing is controlled by lights; a zebra crossing is controlled by pedestrian priority and flashing amber beacons.

column1: What does an island in the centre of a pedestrian crossing mean?
column2: Treat each side of a zebra crossing as a separate crossing; a staggered pelican crossing also counts as two crossings.

column1: What do the white zig-zag lines at a zebra crossing mean?
column2: No overtaking and no parking.

column1: What is the speed limit on national roads and on motorways?
column2: National roads are generally 100 km/h; motorways are generally 120 km/h unless signs say otherwise.

column1: What are the speed limits in built-up areas?
column2: Usually 50 km/h unless a special limit such as 30 km/h or 60 km/h is posted.

column1: What is the minimum tread depth on tyres?
column2: 1.6 mm over the central three-quarters of the tread.

column1: What are the rules regarding bus lanes?
column2: A with-flow bus lane runs with the traffic and can be used by buses, taxis, and bicycles during the stated times; a contra-flow bus lane is generally for buses only unless signs also authorise cyclists.

column1: How far away should you park from a junction?
column2: At least 5 metres away.

column1: What position would you take up for a right turn in a one-way street?
column2: As close as practicable to the right-hand side.

column1: What are hatched markings?
column2: Diagonal or chevron markings used to separate or guide traffic; you must not enter the area they cover.

column1: What does a yield sign mean?
column2: Give way to traffic with priority and do not proceed unless it is safe.

column1: What is a filter light?
column2: A green or amber arrow that lets you proceed in the direction of the arrow if it is safe.

column1: You are approaching traffic lights and they change to amber. What should you do?
column2: Stop unless it is unsafe to do so.

column1: What does a flashing amber traffic light mean?
column2: Proceed with caution if the crossing or junction is clear; pedestrians have priority.

column1: What do flashing red traffic lights mean?
column2: Stop; a train is approaching or the crossing is operating.

column1: What does a continuous yellow line at the side of a road mean?
column2: No parking during certain hours as shown.

column1: What do double continuous yellow lines at the side of the road mean?
column2: No parking at any time.

column1: Give examples of where you would not park.
column2: Near bends, hill crests, hump-back bridges, continuous white lines, entrances, narrow roads, taxi ranks, junctions, bus stops, or on a footpath.

column1: Within what distance from a pedestrian crossing should you not park?
column2: Within 15 metres before it or 5 metres after it.

column1: What procedure must you adopt if crossing a dual carriageway with a narrow central median?
column2: Wait until you can complete the whole crossing safely if the median is too narrow for your vehicle.

column1: What are the differences between a motorway and a dual carriageway?
column2: Motorways have special rules, left-side exits, no crossroads, no roundabouts, and no ordinary traffic lights; a 120 km/h limit may apply on motorways.

column1: Who has priority at an unmarked crossroads with roads of equal importance?
column2: Traffic from the right and traffic already on the junction.

column1: What are the road markings for no entry?
column2: A continuous and a broken white line with the words NO ENTRY.

column1: What would you look out for on country roads?
column2: Pedestrians, cyclists, animals, mud, concealed entrances, bends, and slow-moving farm machinery.

column1: When being overtaken, what must you not do?
column2: Increase your speed.

column1: Where would you never make a U-turn?
column2: In a one-way street, where continuous white lines apply, or where a sign prohibits it.

column1: What is meant by tailgating?
column2: Driving too close to the vehicle in front.

column1: What human factors can affect your driving?
column2: Alcohol, drugs, tiredness, fatigue, anger, attitude, and poor concentration.

column1: What is coasting and why is it potentially dangerous?
column2: Coasting is driving with the clutch down or the gear lever in neutral; it reduces your control of the vehicle.

column1: Who is responsible for seat belts?
column2: The driver is responsible for passengers under 17; passengers aged 17 and over are responsible for themselves.

column1: When following the road ahead on a multi-lane dual carriageway, which lane would you normally use?
column2: Lane 1, the left-hand driving lane, unless signs or road markings say otherwise.

column1: What is the 2 second rule?
column2: A way to judge safe following distance: at least 2 seconds in dry conditions, at least 4 in wet conditions, and more in ice.
